::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Essay, November 2026.** A short, personal essay, written the morning after two claimed proofs of the Riemann hypothesis appeared on the same day. Neither has been confirmed, and this essay does not judge either one. I can't. It is about what the day may change in how we do mathematics. The facts about the two claims come from press reports of 20 November 2026, and I say whose. The second figure is computed; the others are drawings of my own. The code that draws them is linked under each one.
:::

**In short.** On the same day, two proofs of the most famous open problem in mathematics were announced. One was made in 41 days with an AI, Claude, and so far only a computer has checked it. The other was written by hand over twelve years, and it runs to 940 pages. I find this amazing, and I think it will change how mathematics is done. But I don't think it removes mathematics, or us. What struck me is that both proofs are long. That is normal: the first proof of a hard theorem is usually long, and the short one comes later. So here is my bet. Machines will give us more long proofs, faster than ever. Our part will be to find the short ones inside them. I can't prove that a short proof always exists. But I believe we live in a universe that can be described simply, and that bet has paid off before. One honest doubt remains. Machines may be strongest where there is already a lot to learn from, and some conjectures will need mathematics that does not exist yet. Inventing it, I think, is the same work as finding the short proof.

## 1. Two proofs before breakfast

This morning, a little before eight, I was reading LinkedIn on my phone. A professor of mathematics had posted a summary of the day before. Its title was *Two Riemann Proofs, One Day.* I read it twice.

Here is what happened, as reported. Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, announced that he and Claude had proved the Riemann hypothesis, and a wider version of it too. It took 41 days. There is no paper. There is a short note, and an archive of 175,187 files written in Lean. Lean is a programming language in which a computer checks every step of a proof. In a footnote, he says that a full version written out in prose ran past 250,000 pages, and that he chose not to post it. Andrew Sutherland, a mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, built the archive on his own computers. It compiles: the machine accepts every step. The next check, that the final statement really says what the Riemann hypothesis says, was still under way [@sciam2026alpoge; @officechai2026].

A few hours later, Ravi Vakil, the president of the American Mathematical Society, posted a second claim. It is a 940-page manuscript called *The Music of the Primes*, by a young mathematician, Alessandro Masullo. Twelve years of work, all human, no AI. Brian Conrad at Stanford has been reading it closely for months. The plan had been to polish it quietly for a year. The first announcement changed that, so the draft went out as it was [@techcrunch2026; @nacionale2026]. Conrad was careful. To judge the method, he said, the paper must reach a more final version. It is "undergoing major revision" [@sciam2026alpoge]. An early audit posted online already claims serious problems in it; that is not confirmed either [@refine2026].

So, two proofs, and neither is confirmed. The professor ended the post with a question: what is a proof for? I wrote a short comment under it. This essay is that comment, given a bit more room.

## 2. What both proofs are about

The Riemann hypothesis is 167 years old. Bernhard Riemann stated it in 1859, in a paper of about ten pages [@riemann1859]. It is about the prime numbers: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, the numbers that can only be divided by one and by themselves.

If you count the primes as you go up, the count climbs like a staircase. Each prime is a step. The steps look irregular. But from far away, the staircase follows a smooth curve, one that Gauss guessed as a teenager. Riemann found that the gap between the staircase and the curve is controlled by a special function, the zeta function. More exactly, by the places where it is zero. Each zero adds a small wave, like a note in a chord. Together, the notes play the primes. That is why Masullo called his manuscript *The Music of the Primes*.

![**Figure 2.** What both proofs are about. Top: the number of primes up to x climbs like a staircase, close to a smooth curve (the offset logarithmic integral, Gauss's guess). Bottom: the size of the Riemann zeta function along the line where the real part is one half. Each place where it touches zero, marked with a dot, is one of the "notes" that shapes the staircase. The hypothesis says that all the interesting zeros lie on this one line. Computed with mpmath; code in [figs.py](figs.py).](figures/fig02.svg){fig-alt="Two charts, one above the other, under the title: What both proofs are about. The top chart, titled The primes climb like a staircase, close to a smooth curve, shows a blue staircase counting the primes from 2 to 200, reaching 46, and an amber smooth curve, Gauss's smooth guess, running just above it. The bottom chart, titled The zeros of the zeta function, the notes that tune the staircase, shows a blue curve, the size of the zeta function along the critical line, for heights from 0 to 50. It rises and falls in arches and touches zero ten times, each zero marked with an amber dot, the first at 14.13."}

The hypothesis says that all these notes sit on one straight line. Computers have checked trillions of them, and every one is on the line [@platt2021]. But checking is not proving. Nobody has shown that it must be so for all of them. If it is true, many things we believe about the primes become certain. Hundreds of results in mathematics begin with the words "assuming the Riemann hypothesis".

So this is not just another puzzle. It is the problem many mathematicians would pick if they could solve only one.

## 3. Both are long, and that is normal

What struck me first was not the machine. It was the length. One proof runs to 940 pages by hand. The other ran to more than 250,000 pages when the machine tried to write it out in prose. So length is not only a machine habit. People do it too.

And there is a reason. The first proof of a hard theorem is almost always long. The first person through a forest does not walk in a straight line. They go around, they backtrack, they cut through brambles. The straight path is found later, by people who already know where the other side is.

The prime number theorem is my favourite example, because it is about the same staircase. It says that the staircase follows Gauss's curve. Jacques Hadamard and Charles de la Vallée Poussin proved it in 1896, each on their own, with heavy tools. Hadamard's paper was 22 pages [@hadamard1896]. In 1980, Donald Newman found a proof that fits in four pages of a journal for students and teachers [@newman1980]. Don Zagier later showed it could be told even more briefly [@zagier1997]. Eighty-four years, from a forest to a path.

There are other stories like it. In 1976, Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken proved the four colour theorem with a computer checking more than a thousand cases, one by one [@appel1977]. Many mathematicians were uneasy: they could not check it by hand. Almost thirty years later, Georges Gonthier checked the whole proof in a proof assistant, a program that verifies every step [@gonthier2008]. The proof of the Kepler conjecture, about the best way to stack oranges, went the same way. Referees could not fully check it, so Thomas Hales and his colleagues checked it by machine [@hales2017].

So the long proof is not new. What is new is the speed. A machine can now walk through the forest in 41 days instead of twelve years.

## 4. "Then we are finished"

Now, here is the strongest objection, and I want to give it its full weight.

It goes like this. If a machine can prove the Riemann hypothesis in 41 days, what is left for mathematicians? Twelve years of a life against six weeks of a computer. The machine will not stop at one problem. It will take the next one, and the next. Soon, the human proof will be a hobby, like knitting your own socks. Beautiful, but not needed.

I feel the force of this. And I understand why Masullo wrote, in his introduction, to the mathematician "who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate". His answer: "We are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere" [@techcrunch2026].

I agree with him, but for a reason that has less to do with defiance. It has to do with what a proof is for.

A proof does two jobs. The first is to convince us that a statement is true. A machine can now do that job, and do it better than we can: it does not get tired at page 600. The second job is to make us understand *why* it is true. That second job is the one that moves mathematics forward. The understanding is what you carry to the next problem.

William Thurston, one of the great geometers of the last century, said it more clearly than I can. He wrote: "We are not trying to meet some abstract production quota of definitions, theorems and proofs. The measure of our success is whether what we do enables people to understand and think more clearly and effectively about mathematics" [@thurston1994].

A proof of 175,187 files that nobody can read does the first job. It does not yet do the second. Alpöge himself, as reported, has not yet mastered all the mathematics around it [@officechai2026]. That is not a criticism. It is the honest state of a first proof. The forest has been crossed. Nobody has drawn the map yet.

So I don't think we are finished. I think our work changes. Less time hacking through the brambles. More time looking at the path the machine took, and asking: what was the idea? Where did it really turn? What could we throw away?

## 5. The two routes need each other

Here is the picture I had in mind when I wrote my comment. The two proofs that appeared on the same day are not rivals. Each one needs exactly what the other one has.

![**Figure 4.** The two routes need each other. A machine's proof is checked but too long to read; people can distil it, looking for the idea inside. A human proof is full of ideas but not yet checked; machines can check it, every line, in Lean. Both roads lead to the same place: a short proof that is checked, and that one mind can hold. Schematic, my own; code in [figs.py](figs.py).](figures/fig04.svg){fig-alt="A diagram titled The two routes need each other. On the left, two boxes. The upper one, blue, reads: The machine's proof, checked by a computer, too long to read. The lower one, amber, reads: The human proof, readable, full of ideas, not yet checked. On the right, one dark box reads: A short proof, checked, and one mind can hold it. An amber arrow goes from the machine's proof to the short proof, labelled: people distil it, find the idea inside. A blue arrow goes from the human proof to the short proof, labelled: machines check it, every line, in Lean."}

Masullo's 940 pages need checking. Conrad has spent months on them, and still the paper is under major revision. Machines could help here: turn the 940 pages into Lean, step by step, and let the computer find the gaps. That is exactly what happened with the four colour theorem and the Kepler conjecture, only it took years. It could now take weeks.

Alpöge's 175,187 files need the opposite. They need people to read them, not line by line, but the way a hiker reads a map. Where does the path climb? Where does it turn? Which loop was a detour? Machines can help with that too. But deciding which idea is the *real* one, the one worth teaching, is a judgement about what matters. I think that judgement stays with us for a long time.

So the change is not bad. It is a new division of work. The machine is a tireless explorer. We become the cartographers.

## 6. My bet: it must be simpler

Now I have to be honest. Everything above assumes that a short proof of the Riemann hypothesis exists. I don't know that. Nobody does.

Logic even warns us. In 1936, Kurt Gödel noted that some true statements have only very long proofs in a given system, far longer than anyone could write. Step into a stronger system, a wider point of view, and the same statements can have short proofs [@godel1936]. So there is no guarantee that every theorem has a short proof. And the Riemann hypothesis might be one of the long ones.

But look at what Gödel's own result says. The proof became short when the point of view changed. Not when someone worked harder in the same place. I find that hopeful.

And here is where I am provocative, I know. I don't have the answer. I am not a mathematician. But I believe we live in a universe that can be described simply. Not because simplicity is guaranteed, but because it has worked so often that it would be strange if it stopped now. A few equations describe light. A few more describe gravity. The physicist Eugene Wigner called this "the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences" [@wigner1960]. G. H. Hardy wrote that "there is no permanent place in the world for ugly mathematics" [@hardy1940]. Paul Erdős liked to joke that God keeps a book with the most elegant proof of every theorem. Two mathematicians, Martin Aigner and Günter Ziegler, even tried to write some of its pages down [@aigner2018].

The primes are the most basic objects in arithmetic. Count them, and you get a staircase that a smooth curve follows almost perfectly. Something that orderly, I believe, must have a reason that can be said in a few pages. Maybe not today. Maybe not by me. But the long proofs are, I think, the first step toward it, not the last.

I wrote about this feeling before, in a different setting. One evening I read a physics paper I could not follow. A voice in my head said: *it must be simpler than this* ([It Must Be Simpler Than This](../../posts/2026-11-08-it-must-be-simpler-than-this/index.qmd)). A 250,000-page proof gives me exactly the same feeling. Not that it is wrong. That it is not finished.

## 7. Where the data runs out

There is a second challenge, and this one I raise against myself. Machines may be very good at finding solutions where there is already a lot of material around the problem. It may be different for a conjecture whose proof needs mathematics that does not exist yet.

The Riemann hypothesis is not virgin ground. It is one of the most studied problems in mathematics. There is a huge literature around it, trillions of zeros computed, decades of partial results, and a large library of mathematics already written in Lean. A machine that works on it works inside a map that people drew. It has examples to learn from, tools to reuse, and a checker that tells it when it is wrong.

Some conjectures need something that is on no map yet. History has many of these moments. To understand why some equations have no formula for their solutions, Évariste Galois had to invent a new idea, what we now call a group. To prove Fermat's Last Theorem, Andrew Wiles had to prove a large part of a bridge between two distant parts of mathematics. Others had only guessed that the bridge was there. In those cases, the hard part was not to search longer. It was to see the problem in a language that did not exist yet.

I don't know whether machines can do that. Maybe they already do it, somewhere inside those 175,187 files, and nobody has seen it yet. If so, the people who distil the proof will be the first to find out, and that would be the biggest news of all. But it may also be that machines are at their best where there is a lot to learn from, and weaker where there is nothing like it. I said something close to this in April, and I was partly wrong ([Partly Wrong, Mostly Right](../../posts/2026-11-20-partly-wrong-mostly-right/index.qmd)). So I hold it loosely.

Here is what strikes me, though. Remember Gödel: the proof became short when the point of view changed. Very often, a new piece of mathematics is exactly that, a new point of view that makes an old difficulty disappear. If so, the work I am betting on is finding the short proof. The work machines may find hardest is inventing new mathematics. And those may be one and the same work. That is not a reason to relax. It is a reason to keep doing mathematics ourselves.

## 8. What a proof is for

So here is where I land, the morning after.

I think what happened yesterday is great. A machine may have crossed a forest that people have walked around for 167 years. And on the same day, a person crossed it too, by hand, after twelve years. Whatever the verdicts, I find both amazing. It will change how mathematics is done tomorrow. More proofs will be found by machines, and more of them will be checked by machines.

But I don't think it removes mathematics, or us. It changes our job. The first proof tells us *that* something is true. The short proof tells us *why*. Finding the short one has always been human work, and I think the long machine proofs will give us more of that work, not less.

The professor asked what a proof is for. My answer is the one I wrote under the post, a little before eight this morning. A proof is for turning a truth into an idea that one mind can hold.

The machine wrote the first draft. Now comes the part where we make it short.
